title: SELinux Labels, Denials, and Least-privilege Policy

scout.purpose: Master selinux labels, denials, and least-privilege policy through a production or platform contract supported by causal evidence.
scout.realWorldUse: Specialist Android work must remain compatible, secure, measurable, accessible, distributable, and operable outside a demonstration.
scout.outcome: You can design, inspect, test, release, and defend selinux labels, denials, and least-privilege policy.

blocks.text: Android SELinux enforces mandatory access control even for root processes. Policy decisions relate source context, target context, object class, and permission under default deny. Type enforcement confines services and data; file, service, property, device, and other contexts assign labels. DAC permission or Linux capability does not bypass SELinux. Enforcing mode blocks denied operations, while permissive logs them and removes the containment needed for valid testing.

blocks.text: Treat an avc denial as evidence of a disputed access, not an instruction to paste audit2allow output. Confirm the intended architecture, correct labeling, owning domain, Binder or HAL boundary, and whether the access should exist. Fix wrong labels before granting access. Write the narrowest rule and use neverallow constraints to protect invariants. Do not grant broad device, proc, sysfs, file, execute, or service-manager access to silence boot logs. Separate platform and vendor policy compatibility.

blocks.code: adb shell ps -AZ | grep droidquest; adb shell ls -lZ /data/system/droidquest; adb shell dmesg | grep "avc: denied"
blocks.caption: A focused fragment whose complete contract includes exact versions, ownership, adverse paths, compatibility, and release evidence.

blocks.text: Reproduce on enforcing userdebug, capture complete denial, inspect ps -Z and ls -Z, trace domain transition, run policy analysis and relevant tests, then verify no broader access. Test clean install or image, boot, upgrade, recovery, multiple users, adversarial paths, and CTS or VTS policy tests. Document threat model and residual privilege. Policy is production code: review ownership, compatibility, performance, and rollback with the service change.

Expert engineering makes assumptions, authority, compatibility, security, privacy, accessibility, performance, distribution, and recovery reviewable. Begin with a concrete user or platform outcome, identify trust and lifecycle boundaries, and retain exact source, dependency, toolchain, configuration, model or platform version, and artifact identity. Test realistic success plus denial, offline, process death, cancellation, corruption, version skew, resource pressure, and dependency failure. Measure representative distributions rather than best runs. Document unsupported cases, residual risk, owners, release gates, incident response, deprecation, and rollback or roll-forward. A specialised solution is production-ready only when another team can integrate, verify, operate, upgrade, disable, and remove it safely.

trap_check.mistake: Generating and accepting every audit2allow suggestion converts observed behavior into broad authority without checking labels or architecture.
trap_check.why: It hides an ownership, compatibility, trust, lifecycle, or evidence gap that becomes costly outside the demonstration.
trap_check.fix: Make the disputed boundary explicit and add a representative negative or compatibility test plus operational response.

trap_check.mistake: Treating one successful device, client, model, platform build, or release as proof of the supported contract.
trap_check.why: Advanced Android ecosystems contain version, hardware, consumer, policy, and runtime variation.
trap_check.fix: Define the support matrix and verify exact artifacts across representative and adverse conditions.

challenge_intro.task: Diagnose a service denial, correct labels or boundary, add the minimum rule if justified, prove enforcing boot and negative access, and run policy tests.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: The work includes a minimal coherent implementation, exact evidence, support and threat boundaries, adverse testing, release operation, and recovery.

recall.prompt: What four elements identify a basic SELinux access decision?
recall.answer: Source type, target type, object class, and requested permission.

recall.prompt: What must accompany an expert Android artifact?
recall.answer: Exact source and build identity, supported versions, contracts, tests, measurements, security and privacy review, release evidence, owner, and recovery plan.
They prevent consumers and operators from treating an untested or impossible condition as a silent guarantee.
